common_name: Contrast in Styles Siberian Iris (Award of Merit Wine-Red Bitone with Milky Blue Style Arms)

planting.note: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; unlike bearded iris, Siberian iris rhizomes need no rhizome exposure at planting and tolerate wetter soil and less frequent division over time.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Registered by hybridizer Robert Hollingworth in 1989, Contrast in Styles takes its name from the striking two-part color break between its mid-wine standards and falls, each accented with a blue center line or band, and the pale, milky blue style arms that contrast sharply against the wine-red ground — an unusual style-arm color break rarely seen among Siberian iris cultivars. Midseason bloom stalks carry the ruffled flowers above narrow, grass-like clumps of foliage that remain attractive as a textural accent long after bloom ends. The cultivar earned an Award of Merit from the American Iris Society in 1995 after first receiving an Honorable Mention in 1991, cementing its reputation among Siberian iris enthusiasts. It tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and is far less prone to rot and borer problems, making it a lower-maintenance choice for a mixed border or pond edge. Clumps can go many years without needing division; when they do become crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.
sources: American Iris Society Wiki (Iris Encyclopedia) — Siberian Iris Cultivar Registrations

common_name: Gull's Wing Siberian Iris (Late-Blooming Pure White with White Signal)

planting.note: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in spring or early fall in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade; unlike bearded iris, Siberian iris rhizomes need no rhizome exposure at planting and tolerate wetter, more consistently moist soil.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Registered in 1989 by William McGarvey (hybridized by J. Wadekamper) as seedling McG 1861, Gull's Wing is a tall, pure white self with a matching white signal patch, its clean, unmarked color giving the ruffled flowers a luminous, ghostly quality at dusk. It is among the later-blooming Siberian iris cultivars, extending the white-flowered display after earlier selections like White Swirl have finished, atop clumps of narrow, grass-like foliage that stay attractive as a textural accent through summer. The cultivar received an Honorable Mention from the American Iris Society in 1992. It tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and is far less prone to rot and borer problems, making it a lower-maintenance choice for a mixed border, white garden, or pond edge. Clumps can go many years without needing division; when they do become crowded, dig and divide in early fall or right after spring bloom.
sources: American Iris Society Wiki (Iris Encyclopedia) — Siberian Iris Cultivar Registrations

common_name: Flowers Muscadine Grape (Historic Black Female Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant dormant rooted cuttings or container vines in late winter to early spring on a sturdy arbor or high-wire trellis in full sun; Flowers is female-flowered and must be planted alongside a self-fertile cultivar such as Carlos or Cowart for a full crop.

directions: Flowers is one of the oldest named muscadine selections still passed down in Southern gardens, historically grouped with early favorites like James and Thomas for its vigor, reliability, and dessert-quality fruit well before formal university breeding programs began. The medium-to-large berries ripen black with the deep, musky-sweet flavor prized in traditional muscadine cookery, fresh eating, and homemade wine. Because Flowers produces only female flowers, it sets little or no fruit without a nearby self-fertile cultivar such as Carlos or Cowart to provide pollen. This tough, long-lived heirloom vine tolerates the heat, humidity, and disease pressure of the Gulf South with minimal spraying once established on a strong arbor or high-wire trellis.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Muscadine Grape Varieties
